newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Bolger and Hashimoto in wide-ranging talks.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Bolger and Hashimoto in wide-ranging talks.

text.p: World trade, regional security and political developments in Asia and the Pacific are on the agenda at a meeting on Wednesday between Prime Minister Jim Bolger and his Japanese counterpart Ryutaro Hashimoto.

The Japanese prime minister arrived late on Tuesday night for a one-day official visit to New Zealand centred on an hour of formal talks with Bolger on Wednesday morning, lunch in the Beehive and a news conference early afternoon.
It is the first time a Japanese prime minister has visited Wellington since 1974, although two have made trips to Auckland.
Speaking in Parliament yesterday, Bolger said New Zealand and Japan had an excellent bilateral relationship and discussions would focus on international economic and political issues.
Questioned by opposition MPs, he said there was no formal agenda for the talks but he expected two areas of difference -- nuclear waste shipments and whaling -- would come up.

However, he played down the significance of prickly issues between the two countries saying "our relationship is sufficiently mature to have constructive exchanges on areas where there are differences of opinion".
He also said he would reaffirm the coalition Government's policy on foreign investment.

Labour's finance spokesman Michael Cullen had asked whether he would assure Hashimoto that "anti-Asian and anti-investment views" expressed last year by New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, now deputy prime minister and treasurer, were not government policy.

"I have read speeches by the treasurer where he has indicated very positively that the coalition Government welcomes investment in New Zealand, and certainly welcomes investment in New Zealand from Japan," Bolger said.
"I will reaffirm that to Mr Hashimoto."
Bolger was also expected to reaffirm New Zealand's support for Japan's bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council.
Hashimoto was to have met Labour leader Helen Clark and Peters, but late on Tuesday it was announced that those engagements had been cancelled to lighten the Japanese prime minister's tight schedule.
He is due to leave Wellington for Tokyo on Wednesday night.
